title: The index-investing fund manager who bet his fortune on his company's stock
dek: Ben knew ‘don't concentrate on employer stock’is common sense, yet still transferred his PWL equity (acquired by OneDigital) there—he says this is the idiosyncratic risk he actively chose, because he's a company participant, not a salaried bystander.
why: Two PWL advisors publicly disclose their real holdings for the first time and explain why they diverge from ‘theoretical optimality’—for those wanting to know how professionals actually invest, not for template seekers.
who: Investors and professionals curious how professional financial advisors actually allocate their own wealth and balance ‘theoretical optimality’with ‘personal comfort’.
skip: The Apple Podcasts listener Q&A segment at the end (about QQQI fund) is low information density and can be skipped.

points.h: Smart investors hire advisors to save stress, not save money
points.body: Simon Berube, a cardiologist, fully understands passive investing evidence and theoretically could DIY. But he says that as complexity rises—family, insurance, multiple accounts, multiple entities—‘time, errors, and mistakes compound exponentially’and small oversights become big problems decades later. What he needs isn't judgment being replaced—he still constantly asks ‘where's the evidence’—but what Brady calls ‘expert knowledge, integration, and oversight’. This shows that evidence-literate people still pay for advisors, not because advisors pick funds, but because they integrate all the moving pieces without error.

points.h: Income and happiness correlate at only 0.09
points.body: Ben cites 2018 research: the satiation point for life satisfaction in North America was around $105,000 in that sample, equivalent to approximately $137,000 in today's purchasing power; the satiation point for daily emotional happiness was lower, around $85,000. But subsequent 2021 and 2023 research overturned the ‘satiation point’narrative—for most people, happiness rises steadily with income, only the already-unhappy hit a plateau. Even so, the correlation coefficient between income and happiness is only 0.09—the median happiness gap between households earning $15,000 and $250,000 is only 5 points on a 100-point scale.

points.h: His online critics forced him to read academic research
points.body: During his master's, Ben briefly sold insurance and actively managed funds. When he admitted in a media interview that he invested in Fidelity Dividend Plus Fund, the comments section ridiculed him harshly. This shock drove him to research active funds for the first time—tracing back to 1968, decades of evidence consistently showed active funds couldn't beat the index, the opposite of what the industry taught him. Later, learning the Fama-French three-factor model in class, he excitedly called Dimensional about using their products but was told he wasn't qualified to sell them; he briefly despaired and considered returning home to find engineering work. Weeks later, Dimensional called back and introduced him to Cameron Passmore, an Ottawa advisor using their products—leading him to join PWL.

points.h: Same evidence led them to different portfolio allocations
points.body: Ben's main holding is Dimensional Global Equity Portfolio, 100% stocks, zero bonds; Dan holds a 70% stocks / 30% bonds ETF mix. Both accept the same evidence—the Cederberg paper Dan cites also supports a global allocation of roughly one-third domestic stocks—but different risk tolerance led to different final allocations. Dan's principle: ‘take exactly the risk you need, no more and no less’. He did financial planning and found that 70/30 suffices for his retirement spending needs; additional stock exposure buys only ‘a bigger portfolio but not necessarily more happiness’.

points.h: He chose to stake his net worth on company equity
points.body: Ben's private equity isn't a fund but equity in PWL (later acquired by OneDigital) that he holds directly—no fund manager, no layered fees. He admits it violates the conventional wisdom ‘don't concentrate in employer stock’and admits this is the ‘idiosyncratic risk’he actively wanted, because he's an actual contributor to company growth, not a salaried bystander. Dan adds that what matters isn't the percentage of holdings relative to net worth, but whether you've already earmarked enough for ‘how much diversification your financial goals require’—the framework they used helping Shopify employees make concentration decisions: first determine how much diversification your goals need, then do whatever you want with the rest.

points.h: Both agree homebuying was their worst financial decision
points.body: Both Ben and Dan bought homes during the 2020 pandemic and both admit it was the worst investment they've made from a purely financial perspective—Ben says if he hadn't bought then and had kept the money in liquid assets to buy more PWL equity, the difference would be ‘a very large number’; Dan says if he'd invested his down payment in the bull market of the past six years, his portfolio would be 50% to 60% larger. But neither regrets it: homes lock in long-term housing costs, like a long-term bond tied to that specific home's living expenses, and both genuinely like their homes.

points.h: 100% stocks on paper but actually holding a cash buffer
points.body: Ben says his liquid investment portfolio, aside from private equity and his home, is entirely a 100% stocks fund—but he admits his high-yield savings account holds cash equal to roughly 5% of liquid assets, more than he needs daily, purely to ‘not worry’. Dan points out this is an overlooked detail: many who claim to be ‘100% stocks’aren't, because as long as you keep emergency cash, your real stock exposure is already discounted.

points.h: Suboptimal decisions can still be rational ones
points.body: At the show's end, Dan distinguishes ‘suboptimal’from ‘irrational’: homebuying, keeping cash, betting on employer equity are none of them theoretically optimal financial choices, but as long as you've thought through the tradeoffs and opportunity costs before deciding, they're still rational. Ben adds that the show's original intent was always to first explain what's theoretically optimal, then honestly explain why people diverge from it—because a good life doesn't depend only on an optimal portfolio, and ‘an optimal portfolio’itself has no consensus definition.

I'm a health doctor, you're a wealth doctor. The same principle do apply, and compounding also exists in both cases.
But it provides expertise, integration, and oversight that in my daily life with family, job, and lack of interest, to be honest, regarding certain aspects of it.
The correlation between life evaluation or experience happiness and income is 0.09.
But instead of getting my name out there in a good way, I got absolutely eviscerated in the comment section.
Equity in PWL though, and now OneDigital, has been by far my most successful investment.
